title: CascadePoint Private Deployment Connectivity Intake
summary: Intro intake to evaluate Redwood Private for sensitive ML workloads. Main topics: VPC topology, inter-region constraints, private endpoints, egress controls, KMS integration and audit logs. Customer has strict CIDR and peering policies and wants pilot in eu-west-1 and us-east-1.
action_items: Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): share internal diagram for Private deployment modes and required route table changes (due 2027-10-28)
Maya Chen (Redwood AE): send pricing estimate and dedicated vs private comparison doc (due 2027-10-27)
Marco Espino (Customer): confirm CIDR ranges for prod and staging VPCs and share network diagram (due 2027-10-29)
Rina Gupta (Customer): pull SOC2 and encryption-at-rest docs and note any additional compliance controls (due 2027-10-29)
next_steps: Schedule 1-hour technical workshop with customer network team and Redwood infra engineers (propose 2027-11-02)
Run quick PoC connectivity smoke test for eu-west-1 with small model instance (Redwood to provision test host)
Exchange KMS key policies and confirm HSM requirement (if any)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (VP Platform), Rina Gupta (Security Architect), Marco Espino (Cloud Network Eng)

Summary (auto-gen): Initial intake to understand CascadePoint's requirements for a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood. Focus on networking topology, peering options, private endpoints, egress and region restrictions, and KMS integration.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone — thanks for joining, I'm Maya, AE on the account. Diego from our infra SE team is with me. Can we do quick intros?
[00:08] Liam O'Neill: Yeah hi I'm Liam, I run platform at CascadePoint.
[00:11] Rina Gupta: Rina, security architect, I'll be looking at compliance and key mgmt.
[00:15] Marco Espino: Marco, networking — I'll be doing the VPC and peering work.
[00:19] Diego Ramos: Great, thanks. Quick agenda — understand your current cloud topology, constraints (CIDR, regions), what you need for private endpoints, and any compliance gates. We'll talk options: VPC peering, transit gateway, private endpoints, and egress patterns.

[02:05] Liam O'Neill: To set context — CascadePoint is migrating sensitive telemetry processing to our own infra. We want model inference to run on private infra, no internet accessible APIs, and logs must go into our SIEM. We're evaluating Redwood Private. Main blockers: cross-region data residency (eu-west-1 first), and strict no-overlap CIDR policy — we use /16s heavily.

[03:10] Maya Chen: Understood. On region: Redwood Private supports private deployments across multiple regions; for hosted we have multi-region but your requirement sounds like Private with VPC peering or transit. Diego, would you say transit gateway is generally the recommended pattern for multi-VPC/multi-region?
[03:29] Diego Ramos: Yeah, generally we recommend an AWS Transit Gateway for scale if you have many VPCs and want central routing. For a simpler setup, VPC peering is fine if it's limited (one or two VPCs). Important note: for transit gateway across regions you'll need TGW inter-region attachments which are supported but add cost and require proper route propagation. Also watch for overlapping CIDR — peering/TGW will fail if there is overlap.

[04:45] Marco Espino: We do have overlapping prefixes in some environments, that's why we hated the peering. Our plan was to carve out new /20s for Redwood in each region. Is that possible?
[04:58] Diego Ramos: Yes, you can allocate new non-overlapping ranges, Redwood's footprint in the customer's VPC is usually small — we provide an expected set of CIDRs for subnets, and the private endpoints need interface ENIs in those subnets. We'll send the exact size, but typically a couple of /28s per region plus route entries.

[06:12] Rina Gupta: On the encryption side — we use AWS KMS and are moving toward HSM-backed keys. Does Redwood integrate with customer-managed KMS? We cannot have Redwood-managed keys for production.
[06:28] Diego Ramos: We support customer-managed KMS for data at rest in Private deployments. If you need HSM-level keys we can integrate via CloudHSM/KMS. For audit logs, we can forward service logs to your S3 via VPC endpoints and those can then be ingested into your SIEM. We'll surface the exact IAM and key policy requirements.

[07:10] Liam O'Neill: About endpoints — do you use AWS interface endpoints (ENI) or do we need gateway endpoints? We also have strict egress inspection where everything must go through our firewall.
[07:23] Maya Chen: For Redwood Private we use interface endpoints (AWS interface VPC endpoints) so traffic to Redwood control/management plane is over private ENIs. For egress — if you want deep packet inspection we can route traffic through your egress appliances. There is a control plane vs dataplane split — dataplane is usually local to the customer's VPC or to the dedicated private subnet, and control plane calls can be locked down to your private endpoints. Diego can explain network flow.

[08:18] Diego Ramos: Right. Typical pattern: customer sets up interface endpoints backed by Redwood's private link (or a private IP-based peering for dedicated). Then inference host points to local private IPs. For egress it depends: if the model needs to pull artifacts from external registries you can either mirror artifacts internally (recommended) or allow very limited egress via NAT+firewall rules. We recommend mirroring models into an internal artifact store to avoid outbound dependencies.

[09:55] Marco Espino: We prefer no outbound. We'll mirror images in our ECR. How does Redwood handle image pulling in Private?
[10:04] Diego Ramos: You can either push images to our registries via a secured transfer, or we can run the runtime pulling from your ECR if the deployment is in your VPC. For on-prem or VPC deployments within your network, the runtime will access your ECR over private links. We'll need IAM roles and instance profiles set up for that.

[11:30] Rina Gupta: Audit trails — we need proof of model versioning and who queried what — do you surface token-level logs and user identifiers? We need to tie requests to internal user IDs for compliance.
[11:44] Maya Chen: We have request-level tracing in Redwood Console for Private, and can ship audit logs to your CloudWatch or S3 with request metadata. For PII redaction, we have line items in the security pack; we'll share the security docs.

[12:20] Liam O'Neill: About latency — if we put Redwood runtime in eu-west-1 and our app servers are also in eu-west-1, what's typical p95?
[12:32] Diego Ramos: For small/medium models p95 is sub-200ms for generation tokens in the steady state assuming no heavy batching. For larger models it's higher. We'll provide model-specific perf profiles. Also you can tune batching/kv-cache to optimize for throughput vs latency.

[13:58] Marco Espino: Any adjustments to route tables we need to do? We run strict deny by default and everything goes through a transit VPC inspection stack.
[14:10] Diego Ramos: You'll need to allow traffic to the Redwood service CIDRs in the route table for the subnets hosting the interface endpoints — basically point the route to the ENIs for the interface endpoints. If you're using TGW, ensure route propagation for those attachments. Also security groups on the ENIs should allow from your app subnets. We'll provide exact ports and FQDNs — note that some of the control traffic uses ranges that may change with service updates, so we recommend allowing via interface endpoint and private DNS rather than opening wide CIDR ranges.

[15:40] Rina Gupta: Data residency — we need to ensure inference logs never leave eu-west-1 for EU customers. Can Redwood enforce region-level isolation?
[15:53] Maya Chen: Yes — in Private deployment you can pin model runtime and storage to specific regions. For logs, we can configure local log sinks. Diego: any caveats here?
[16:05] Diego Ramos: We can absolutely isolate regionally. The main caveat is if you want cross-region fallback for reliability, that would require replication or route failover which could move data. If you need strict residency with no cross-region replication, we can restrict fallback and operating region to eu-west-1 only. That may impact SLA in rare infra events.

[17:00] Liam O'Neill: Our legal team will probably balk at any possibility of cross-region failover without encryption and audit. We need explicit guarantees in the SLA.
[17:12] Maya Chen: Noted — we'll flag that for legal. We have enterprise SLA add-ons and can put region restrictions in the contract and run scheduled failover tests.

[18:05] Marco Espino: About private link vs peering — we prefer not to bring up peering because of scale. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is probably preferable for us. Does Redwood support PrivateLink for the control plane?
[18:18] Diego Ramos: Yes, PrivateLink is supported for the control plane and management APIs. For the actual inference dataplane in Private deployments we also support local runtime inside customer VPCs so traffic never touches our public network. Implementation detail: if we host runtime in your VPC using an appliance/AMI, then network is fully under your control. If we host in our dedicated hardware but provide private connectivity, we use private IPs through interconnects — both are options.

[19:40] Rina Gupta: We run a third-party IDS/IPS and every new ENI must be onboarded. How intrusive is the onboarding?
[19:50] Diego Ramos: Minimal — the ENIs created by interface endpoints look like any other ENI. We'll provide a reproducible CloudFormation/Terraform template that creates the endpoints and required SGs so your team can review and vet them. The only additional piece is key exchange and IAM role bindings.

[21:05] Liam O'Neill: Pricing question — does Private include egress fees? If we keep all traffic in-region via PrivateLink, what are the expected costs?
[21:18] Maya Chen: Pricing for Private includes infrastructure and per-hour or per-node costs depending on config. Egress within the same region to private endpoints is usually negligible; cross-region interconnects have charges. We'll include a cost model showing expected monthly infrastructure and transfer costs for eu-west-1 and us-east-1.

[22:47] Marco Espino: We need to map this to our network diagram — Marco shows a diagram link in chat (shared link: https://cascadpoint.example.net/diagrams/runtime-vpc-2027).
[22:59] Maya Chen: Great — we'll pull that. Please ensure the diagram includes the CIDR blocks for each VPC and the TGW usage.

[24:10] Rina Gupta: One more thing — our compliance requires SAML SSO for admin console and RBAC for operator accounts. How is Redwood Console authentication handled in Private?
[24:23] Diego Ramos: We support SAML SSO integration for Console and RBAC via our identity system. For Private, the console can be hosted in your network and fronted by your IdP if needed. We'll surface the SAML metadata and required endpoints.

[25:40] Liam O'Neill: Can we do canary deployments and pin model versions? We need the ability to rollback quickly.
[25:51] Maya Chen: Yes, rollouts/canaries are supported in the platform — you can pin model versions and route a percentage of traffic to a variant. In Private deployments the routing is configured through the control plane and enforced locally.

[27:30] Marco Espino: There's also an on-prem data center in DUB that uses ExpressRoute equivalent. Can Redwood support an on-prem connector or would you expect us to bring up a VPN to the Redwood cloud region?
[27:44] Diego Ramos: We support on-prem via either IPSec VPN or direct connect/ExpressRoute circuits. For high-throughput, Direct Connect/ExpressRoute is preferred. For initial PoC a site-to-site VPN is often fine. If you want the runtime fully on-prem, we have an on-prem package but that requires additional planning for hardware and orchestration.

[29:05] Rina Gupta: If we run the runtime on-prem, do you still see request-level logs, or is everything local? We want logs to stay within our SIEM.
[29:18] Diego Ramos: If you opt for fully on-prem, logs remain local and we don't ingest them. For hybrid, we can forward a subset or anonymized metrics to Redwood for billing/health; that's configurable.

[31:00] Liam O'Neill: Ok tactical asks — we want a small PoC: eu-west-1 only, one runtime node, private endpoints, KMS customer-managed keys, logs to S3 and SIEM. Can you give an estimate for time to stand up?
[31:14] Maya Chen: For a basic PoC we can be up in 2-3 weeks assuming network work and keys are provisioned quickly. Diego: anything to add?
[31:22] Diego Ramos: Two-three weeks is realistic: day 0–3 planning, day 4–8 infra changes and endpoint creation, day 9–12 provisioning and smoke test, day 13–15 validation. If there are approvals or change windows on your side it can stretch.

[33:05] Marco Espino: Our change window for prod is only on Sundays at 02:00 UTC — that could delay us. For the PoC we can use a staging VPC with flexible windows.

[34:10] Rina Gupta: On legal side — we need to review patching cadence, vulnerability scan reports, and data access controls. Send those docs and we'll route to security.
[34:21] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll attach Redwood security pack link in follow-up (link: https://redwood.example.com/security-pack).

[35:00] Liam O'Neill: Any particular gotchas with S3 endpoints and bucket policies for logs? We restrict bucket access on prefix and assume role only.
[35:12] Diego Ramos: We'll need an IAM role we can assume to write logs, or you can set a bucket policy that allows our service principal to PutObject to a specific prefix. We'll share the example policy. Also consider S3 VPC endpoints to keep traffic local.

[36:45] Maya Chen: Quick question for Marco — do you have a preferred method for artifact mirroring (ECR replication, or a private registry)?
[36:55] Marco Espino: We prefer ECR with cross-account replication.

[37:05] Diego Ramos: That's fine. We'll need a role for the runtime to pull the images and a trust policy.

[38:40] Rina Gupta: About billing data — we want token-level usage tied to our internal cost center IDs. Can you surface that?
[38:53] Maya Chen: Yes we can emit cost telemetry with metadata tags that map to your cost centers. For Private deployments we can include token-level usage in the billing export. We'll map tags to your internal IDs.

[40:20] Marco Espino: For the PoC, can we do a small latency benchmark? 100 concurrent short requests hitting a small model?
[40:33] Diego Ramos: Yes — we can run a benchmark. Redwood provides a lightweight load generator; we usually do a script that simulates 100 concurrent clients for 10 minutes and produce p50/p95/p99. We'll coordinate the test window with your team.

[42:05] Liam O'Neill: I have one more compliance question — do you have a documented data purge flow? Our GDPR team wants retention guarantees and deletion timelines.
[42:17] Maya Chen: We have documented retention and deletion procedures. For Private we can implement short retention windows or immediate deletion on request. We'll send the retention docs and deletion API spec.

[43:40] Rina Gupta: One operational detail — we rotate keys every 90 days internally. Will that break anything?
[43:50] Diego Ramos: We support key rotation. We'll need to coordinate rotation windows and ensure the runtime has the updated KMS key ARN or alias. If you're re-creating keys you'll need to update the config; using KMS aliases is easier.

[45:10] Marco Espino: Do you have sample Terraform modules for the Private onboarding?
[45:18] Maya Chen: Yes, we have Terraform modules and CloudFormation templates. We'll provide a repo link.

[46:00] Liam O'Neill: Great. What's the preferred next step — workshop?
[46:07] Maya Chen: Yes, propose a 1-hour network workshop to walk through the diagram and run through Terraform. We'll include Diego and an infra engineer. Proposed dates: 2027-11-02 or 2027-11-04.

[46:40] Marco Espino: 11/02 works for us.

[46:50] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll send calendar invite. Last thing — any other blockers we haven't covered?
[47:05] Rina Gupta: Not yet; legal will push a few contract questions after the security docs.
[47:12] Liam O'Neill: We'll validate the CIDR and get that to you.

[48:00] Diego Ramos: Action items recap: we'll send templates for endpoints, SGs, IAM policies, and the perf profile. We'll also include a minimal checklist for the PoC.
[48:15] Maya Chen: And I'll send pricing and the comparison doc for dedicated vs private modes.

[49:00] Liam O'Neill: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[49:06] Marco Espino: Thanks.
[49:08] Rina Gupta: Thanks everyone.
[49:11] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with docs and invite.

[52:00] End of meeting

Notes on transcription: some speaker boundaries may be off; company names and product names occasionally mistranscribed.
